narrative:
The model predicted a 60% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your first-year grades had the strongest influence. Placing in the very bottom decile of your class (compared to an average of 6th decile among accepted students) strongly pushed the prediction toward failure. Your third-year class ranking was the second most important factor; again finishing near the bottom (2nd decile versus an average around 6th) added further weight toward a likely bar exam failure.

Working full-time while in law school was the third most influential piece of information. This actually nudged the prediction slightly toward passing, because most successful students also study full-time. However, this single positive signal was not nearly enough to overcome the much stronger negative impact of your early academic performance.

Taken together, the model concluded that your relatively low grades in the first two years of law school made success on the bar exam less likely than the school is willing to accept.

What you should do next is focus on improving your study methods and academic performance immediately. Raising your class ranking in the remaining years, combined with dedicated bar-prep work, can meaningfully change your trajectory before you retake the exam or reapply.
